parts.title: Part 1
parts.transcript: Parroto IELTS Practice. Listening Test 19. You will hear a number of different recordings, and you will have to answer questions on what you hear. There will be time for you to read the instructions and questions, and you will have a chance to check your work. All the recordings will be played once only. The test is in four parts. Now turn to Part 1. Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a dog training school to ask about classes for his puppy. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5. Now listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5. Sally: Good afternoon, Happy Tails Dog Training. Sally speaking. Mark: Oh, hello. I'm calling to find out about your puppy classes. We've just got a new dog, and I think we need some help. Sally: You're not the only one. That's what most people say when they ring us. Our classes concentrate on basic obedience and on getting puppies used to other dogs and people. How old is your puppy? Mark: He's five months old. He's called Milo. He's very friendly, but he pulls on the lead all the time, and he doesn't always come back when I call him. Sally: That's very normal at that age. He'd go into our Juniors group, which is for puppies between four and eight months. For the first few weeks, the classes take place in a hall, so that the puppies aren't distracted by everything that's going on outside. Then, once they've learned to concentrate, we move out into the field behind the building. Mark: That sounds sensible. He's our first dog, actually. My wife and I both grew up with cats, so this is all quite new to us. Sally: Don't worry. Lots of our owners are first-timers, and they always say how much they learn. Mark: Good. And who runs the classes? Sally: Well, each class has a trainer and an assistant. You'll be able to recognise the trainers easily, because they all wear green jackets. The assistants wear yellow ones. The assistants are often people who are still learning, so if you have a question, it's best to ask the person in green. Mark: OK. And are the trainers qualified? Sally: Yes. They all have a diploma in animal behaviour, which takes two years to complete, and they've all worked with dogs for at least five years before they join us. Mark: And do you offer private lessons as well? Sally: We do, but we usually recommend starting with a group class, because puppies learn a lot from watching each other. Private lessons are more useful later, if there's a particular problem. Mark: That's good to know. How many dogs are there in each class? Sally: We never have more than six, so that everyone gets plenty of attention. Each session lasts an hour, and halfway through, there's a short tea break. That's when owners can chat to the trainer and ask any questions they have, while the puppies have a rest. Mark: Lovely. And what happens if the weather's bad? Do you ever cancel classes? Sally: Hardly ever. Rain doesn't stop us, and even snow isn't usually a problem. The only time we cancel is if there's ice on the roads, because it isn't safe for people to drive here. If that happens, we'll send you a text message. Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10. Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10. Mark: Is there anything I need to bring with me? Sally: Yes. Obviously you'll need a lead and a collar. And please bring some small treats, because we use them to reward the puppies when they do something right. You don't need to bring any toys. We've got plenty of those. Mark: Right. Anything else? Sally: It's a good idea to bring a blanket, or a mat of some kind, for your puppy to lie on. It helps them to settle down when they're not doing an exercise. Oh, and we'll need to see his vaccination record, just to make sure he's up to date. Mark: OK, I'll dig that out. When does the next course start? Sally: Next Tuesday. The classes normally start at seven o'clock in the evening, but on the first evening, please try to get here by quarter to seven, because there are a few things we need to do first. Mark: What sort of things? Sally: Well, the most important is that we check every puppy's microchip, to make sure that it's working and that the details on it are correct. You'd be surprised how often people have moved house and forgotten to update them. Mark: I think ours is fine, but it's good to check. Will the first evening finish later than usual? Sally: No, it'll finish at eight o'clock, the same as all the other classes. So, after the checks, we ask all the owners to go to the office, where you'll fill in a short form about your puppy, and then you'll meet your trainer. Mark: OK. And how much does the course cost? Sally: It's eighty-four pounds for six weeks. That's a little more than last year, when it was seventy-eight, but I'm afraid our costs have gone up. Mark: That's still very reasonable. Can I book a place for Milo now? Sally: Of course. Can I take your name, please? That is the end of Part 1. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 1.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a recruitment consultant giving a talk at a jobs fair about careers in the renewable energy sector. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Speaker: Hello, everyone, and thanks for coming along. My name's Karen Doyle, and I work for GreenPath Recruitment. We specialise in finding people for jobs in renewable energy, which means wind, solar, and other forms of clean power. It's a sector that's growing very fast, and I'd like to explain why it might be the right choice for some of you. Speaker: So, what are the main attractions? Well, firstly, because countries around the world have committed to reducing their carbon emissions, demand for skilled workers in this area is only going to increase. That means that once you've got the right skills, you're unlikely to be out of work for long. For many of the people we place, that long-term security is the most important thing. The other big attraction is that people feel they're doing something that really matters. Many of our candidates tell us that they wanted a job where they could make a difference to the planet, and that's something you can genuinely do in this sector. Speaker: Now, I should be honest about pay. Some jobs, particularly in engineering, are very well paid, but starting salaries in most areas are about average, so don't expect to get rich straight away. And although some jobs involve an office, many of them don't follow regular office hours at all. Speaker: That brings me to the less attractive side of things. Many technical jobs, especially offshore, involve spending two or three weeks at a time away from home, which can be hard if you have a family. And turbines don't only break down between nine and five, so technicians often have to work shifts, including nights and weekends, when urgent repairs are needed. Some people worry about safety, but in fact standards are extremely high, and accident rates are low. And people often ask about the cost of training, but employers usually pay for that. There are also plenty of opportunities for promotion, so that's not usually a concern. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Speaker: Now let me tell you about some of the jobs we're currently recruiting for. The first is for a project coordinator at a young solar company that's growing very quickly. It's a very fast-moving place, and things change from one week to the next, but the staff there have a lot of fun, and the atmosphere is great. You won't be managing anyone at first, but you'll be working closely with the engineers. Speaker: Next, we're looking for an energy analyst for a large electricity supplier. You'll be studying data on energy use and helping to plan where new wind and solar farms should go. It's a large organisation, and people who do well there can move up very quickly. Some of their managers are still in their twenties. Speaker: We also have a vacancy for a community liaison officer. This person will be the link between a wind farm developer and the people living near a planned site, explaining the project and listening to their concerns. It's a contract for twelve months, while the planning process takes place, so it's not permanent, although it might be extended. Speaker: Then there's a sales representative for a company that installs solar panels on people's homes. You'll be visiting customers all over the region to assess their properties and give quotes, so you'll need to be happy driving several hundred miles a week. There's no bonus scheme, but the basic salary is good. Speaker: We're also recruiting for a trainee wind turbine technician. This is a great opportunity for someone who wants to start a new career. You don't need to have worked in the industry before, because full training will be given, although you'll need to be comfortable working at heights. Speaker: And finally, an offshore wind technician, working on a wind farm out at sea. You'll work two weeks on and two weeks off, and during your working period, you'll live on a special vessel next to the wind farm, where accommodation and all meals are provided. You'll need at least two years' experience for this one. Speaker: So, if any of these sound interesting, come and talk to me at our stand afterwards. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students called Leah and Sam starting to plan their presentation on plastic waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Sam: OK, Leah, shall we start getting some ideas together for our presentation on plastic waste? Leah: Sure. I thought I could talk about the experiment I did last term, looking for microplastics in the river near the campus. Sam: That was the one where you filtered water samples and counted the plastic particles under a microscope, wasn't it? Leah: That's right. It was much harder to set up than I'd expected. I collected water from twelve different points along the river, three times a week for two months, so in the end I had nearly three hundred samples to get through. Sam: Wow, that's a lot. Did you find what you expected? Leah: Not really. I'd assumed the amount of plastic would increase as the river got closer to the town, but actually there wasn't much difference. The biggest problem, though, was making sure I didn't add any plastic myself. Sam: What do you mean? Leah: Well, a lot of clothes are made of synthetic materials, and they shed tiny fibres all the time. So I had to wear cotton clothes whenever I was collecting or testing samples, and I used glass jars instead of plastic bottles. Otherwise I might have been counting fibres from my own jumper. I'd also wanted to repeat the whole thing in different seasons, but I didn't have time. Sam: I'd never have thought of that. Anyway, then there's my compost experiment. Leah: Where you tested whether so-called biodegradable bags really break down? Sam: Yes. I buried pieces of five different types of bag in the compost bin behind the science building. My results weren't very convincing, though. Hardly any of the bags had broken down at all. Leah: Maybe that's just what happens. Sam: Possibly, but I think I only left them in the compost for six weeks, which probably wasn't nearly long enough. Most of the manufacturers say it takes at least three months. And I was using a cheap thermometer to check the temperature inside the bin, and I'm not sure the readings were accurate. If the compost wasn't warm enough, that would have slowed everything down. Leah: You could always try it again next year. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Sam: So, what can we say about reducing plastic waste? Leah: Well, there's a lot that supermarkets could do. I read about a study where a supermarket moved its loose fruit and vegetables, the ones without any packaging, to the shelves right by the entrance. Sales of unpackaged produce went up by almost a third, just because people saw them first. Sam: That's interesting. And I think manufacturers could do a lot more too. Have you looked at the recycling symbols on packaging? There are so many different ones, and half of them don't actually mean the item can be recycled. I'm sure they make them confusing on purpose, so that people feel better about buying the product. Leah: I agree. There's one that just means the company has paid into a recycling scheme, but most people think it means you can put it in the recycling bin. Sam: Exactly. And that links to something else I read. When people in the UK are asked how much of their household waste they recycle, the average answer is around seventy per cent. But when researchers actually looked in people's bins, the real figure was much lower, well under half. Leah: So people think they're doing much better than they are. Sam: That's right. So how do we change people's behaviour? Leah: Well, look at the deposit return schemes in countries like Germany and Norway, where you pay a small extra amount for a drink in a plastic bottle and get it back when you return the bottle to a machine in the shop. Return rates there are over ninety per cent. It's a very simple change, but because people get their money back every time, it becomes a habit. Sam: Right. It's amazing what a small practical change can do. Now, what about plastic in the oceans? I've found loads of information about that. Leah: I know, and it's really important, but I'm not sure it fits. Our tutor said we should focus on what individuals and businesses can do in this country, and ocean plastic is such a huge global issue. We'd only have time to scratch the surface. Sam: I suppose you're right. It would make the presentation too broad. Let's leave it out. Leah: OK. So, we've still got an hour before the library closes. What shall we do next? Sam: I think we should decide exactly what we're going to include, and in what order, before we start on the slides. Leah: Good idea. Let's make a list. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer on a graphic design course introducing the subject of handwriting and calligraphy. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something that most of you probably do less and less, and that's writing by hand. For thousands of years, handwriting was the main way in which people recorded information and communicated at a distance. Today, most of us type on keyboards or on our phones, and many adults admit that they hardly ever pick up a pen, apart from signing their name or writing a quick note. Lecturer: In fact, handwriting has come to seem so unimportant that some countries have stopped teaching cursive writing, that's the joined-up style where the letters are linked together, in their schools. The argument was that children's time would be better spent learning to type. But interestingly, in the last few years, the trend seems to have started to reverse. Sales of notebooks have risen steadily, and so have sales of fountain pens, which many people thought had disappeared for good. And calligraphy classes, where people learn to write beautiful decorative letters, are becoming increasingly popular, particularly with young people, who often discover the art through videos online. Lecturer: So why are people returning to handwriting? Well, there's growing evidence that it has real benefits. In one well-known study, university students were asked to take notes during a lecture, either on a laptop or by hand. Those who used laptops wrote down more words, but they tended to copy what the lecturer said word for word. Those who wrote by hand had to be selective, and so they summarised the ideas in their own words. When they were tested afterwards, the students who had written by hand showed a better understanding of the ideas in the lecture. Lecturer: There's also research suggesting that young children who learn letters by writing them, rather than by typing them, are better at recognising those letters later. Some teachers also believe that children write longer and more imaginative stories when they use a pen rather than a keyboard, although this is harder to prove. And many of the people who take up calligraphy say that the main attraction is that it gives them a break from screens. Because it requires such careful concentration, it can be very relaxing, rather like meditation. Lecturer: Now let's go back in time and look at how people wrote in the past. The ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus, a kind of paper made from a plant that grew along the River Nile. To write on it, they used pens made from reeds, which were cut at an angle and sometimes chewed at the end to make a kind of brush. Their ink was usually made from soot, mixed with water and a type of gum. Lecturer: In medieval Europe, the most common writing tool was the quill, a pen made from the feathers of large birds, especially geese. A good quill had to be cut very carefully with a small knife, and it needed to be sharpened again and again as the writer worked. That's where the word penknife comes from. Scribes in this period generally wrote on parchment, which was made from animal skin that had been cleaned, stretched and dried. It was very durable, but it was also very expensive, which is why writing was often very small, with no space wasted. Lecturer: The most widely used ink in Europe for over a thousand years was made from galls. These are small round growths that appear on oak trees when insects lay their eggs in them. When the galls were crushed and mixed with iron salts, they produced a dark ink that soaked into the page and lasted for centuries, although in some cases it has slowly eaten into the page. Lecturer: Of course, the invention of printing in the fifteenth century meant that books no longer had to be copied out by hand. But handwriting remained essential for letters, business and education for another five hundred years. Another interesting point is that, because people in so many different places were writing for so many different purposes, different regions developed their own scripts, with distinctive shapes of letters. This means that experts can often tell where and roughly when a manuscript was written simply by looking at the handwriting. We'll be looking at some examples of these scripts next week, and you'll have the chance to try some of them yourselves. Lecturer: So, before we move on, are there any questions so far? That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.transcript: Part 2. You will hear a recruitment consultant giving a talk at a jobs fair about careers in the renewable energy sector. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 14. Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 14. Speaker: Hello, everyone, and thanks for coming along. My name's Karen Doyle, and I work for GreenPath Recruitment. We specialise in finding people for jobs in renewable energy, which means wind, solar, and other forms of clean power. It's a sector that's growing very fast, and I'd like to explain why it might be the right choice for some of you. Speaker: So, what are the main attractions? Well, firstly, because countries around the world have committed to reducing their carbon emissions, demand for skilled workers in this area is only going to increase. That means that once you've got the right skills, you're unlikely to be out of work for long. For many of the people we place, that long-term security is the most important thing. The other big attraction is that people feel they're doing something that really matters. Many of our candidates tell us that they wanted a job where they could make a difference to the planet, and that's something you can genuinely do in this sector. Speaker: Now, I should be honest about pay. Some jobs, particularly in engineering, are very well paid, but starting salaries in most areas are about average, so don't expect to get rich straight away. And although some jobs involve an office, many of them don't follow regular office hours at all. Speaker: That brings me to the less attractive side of things. Many technical jobs, especially offshore, involve spending two or three weeks at a time away from home, which can be hard if you have a family. And turbines don't only break down between nine and five, so technicians often have to work shifts, including nights and weekends, when urgent repairs are needed. Some people worry about safety, but in fact standards are extremely high, and accident rates are low. And people often ask about the cost of training, but employers usually pay for that. There are also plenty of opportunities for promotion, so that's not usually a concern. Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 15 to 20. Now listen and answer questions 15 to 20. Speaker: Now let me tell you about some of the jobs we're currently recruiting for. The first is for a project coordinator at a young solar company that's growing very quickly. It's a very fast-moving place, and things change from one week to the next, but the staff there have a lot of fun, and the atmosphere is great. You won't be managing anyone at first, but you'll be working closely with the engineers. Speaker: Next, we're looking for an energy analyst for a large electricity supplier. You'll be studying data on energy use and helping to plan where new wind and solar farms should go. It's a large organisation, and people who do well there can move up very quickly. Some of their managers are still in their twenties. Speaker: We also have a vacancy for a community liaison officer. This person will be the link between a wind farm developer and the people living near a planned site, explaining the project and listening to their concerns. It's a contract for twelve months, while the planning process takes place, so it's not permanent, although it might be extended. Speaker: Then there's a sales representative for a company that installs solar panels on people's homes. You'll be visiting customers all over the region to assess their properties and give quotes, so you'll need to be happy driving several hundred miles a week. There's no bonus scheme, but the basic salary is good. Speaker: We're also recruiting for a trainee wind turbine technician. This is a great opportunity for someone who wants to start a new career. You don't need to have worked in the industry before, because full training will be given, although you'll need to be comfortable working at heights. Speaker: And finally, an offshore wind technician, working on a wind farm out at sea. You'll work two weeks on and two weeks off, and during your working period, you'll live on a special vessel next to the wind farm, where accommodation and all meals are provided. You'll need at least two years' experience for this one. Speaker: So, if any of these sound interesting, come and talk to me at our stand afterwards. That is the end of Part 2. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 2.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.transcript: Part 3. You will hear two environmental science students called Leah and Sam starting to plan their presentation on plastic waste. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24. Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 24. Sam: OK, Leah, shall we start getting some ideas together for our presentation on plastic waste? Leah: Sure. I thought I could talk about the experiment I did last term, looking for microplastics in the river near the campus. Sam: That was the one where you filtered water samples and counted the plastic particles under a microscope, wasn't it? Leah: That's right. It was much harder to set up than I'd expected. I collected water from twelve different points along the river, three times a week for two months, so in the end I had nearly three hundred samples to get through. Sam: Wow, that's a lot. Did you find what you expected? Leah: Not really. I'd assumed the amount of plastic would increase as the river got closer to the town, but actually there wasn't much difference. The biggest problem, though, was making sure I didn't add any plastic myself. Sam: What do you mean? Leah: Well, a lot of clothes are made of synthetic materials, and they shed tiny fibres all the time. So I had to wear cotton clothes whenever I was collecting or testing samples, and I used glass jars instead of plastic bottles. Otherwise I might have been counting fibres from my own jumper. I'd also wanted to repeat the whole thing in different seasons, but I didn't have time. Sam: I'd never have thought of that. Anyway, then there's my compost experiment. Leah: Where you tested whether so-called biodegradable bags really break down? Sam: Yes. I buried pieces of five different types of bag in the compost bin behind the science building. My results weren't very convincing, though. Hardly any of the bags had broken down at all. Leah: Maybe that's just what happens. Sam: Possibly, but I think I only left them in the compost for six weeks, which probably wasn't nearly long enough. Most of the manufacturers say it takes at least three months. And I was using a cheap thermometer to check the temperature inside the bin, and I'm not sure the readings were accurate. If the compost wasn't warm enough, that would have slowed everything down. Leah: You could always try it again next year. Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 25 to 30. Now listen and answer questions 25 to 30. Sam: So, what can we say about reducing plastic waste? Leah: Well, there's a lot that supermarkets could do. I read about a study where a supermarket moved its loose fruit and vegetables, the ones without any packaging, to the shelves right by the entrance. Sales of unpackaged produce went up by almost a third, just because people saw them first. Sam: That's interesting. And I think manufacturers could do a lot more too. Have you looked at the recycling symbols on packaging? There are so many different ones, and half of them don't actually mean the item can be recycled. I'm sure they make them confusing on purpose, so that people feel better about buying the product. Leah: I agree. There's one that just means the company has paid into a recycling scheme, but most people think it means you can put it in the recycling bin. Sam: Exactly. And that links to something else I read. When people in the UK are asked how much of their household waste they recycle, the average answer is around seventy per cent. But when researchers actually looked in people's bins, the real figure was much lower, well under half. Leah: So people think they're doing much better than they are. Sam: That's right. So how do we change people's behaviour? Leah: Well, look at the deposit return schemes in countries like Germany and Norway, where you pay a small extra amount for a drink in a plastic bottle and get it back when you return the bottle to a machine in the shop. Return rates there are over ninety per cent. It's a very simple change, but because people get their money back every time, it becomes a habit. Sam: Right. It's amazing what a small practical change can do. Now, what about plastic in the oceans? I've found loads of information about that. Leah: I know, and it's really important, but I'm not sure it fits. Our tutor said we should focus on what individuals and businesses can do in this country, and ocean plastic is such a huge global issue. We'd only have time to scratch the surface. Sam: I suppose you're right. It would make the presentation too broad. Let's leave it out. Leah: OK. So, we've still got an hour before the library closes. What shall we do next? Sam: I think we should decide exactly what we're going to include, and in what order, before we start on the slides. Leah: Good idea. Let's make a list. That is the end of Part 3. You now have thirty seconds to check your answers to Part 3.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.transcript: Part 4. You will hear a lecturer on a graphic design course introducing the subject of handwriting and calligraphy. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40. Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40. Lecturer: Good morning, everyone. Today I want to talk about something that most of you probably do less and less, and that's writing by hand. For thousands of years, handwriting was the main way in which people recorded information and communicated at a distance. Today, most of us type on keyboards or on our phones, and many adults admit that they hardly ever pick up a pen, apart from signing their name or writing a quick note. Lecturer: In fact, handwriting has come to seem so unimportant that some countries have stopped teaching cursive writing, that's the joined-up style where the letters are linked together, in their schools. The argument was that children's time would be better spent learning to type. But interestingly, in the last few years, the trend seems to have started to reverse. Sales of notebooks have risen steadily, and so have sales of fountain pens, which many people thought had disappeared for good. And calligraphy classes, where people learn to write beautiful decorative letters, are becoming increasingly popular, particularly with young people, who often discover the art through videos online. Lecturer: So why are people returning to handwriting? Well, there's growing evidence that it has real benefits. In one well-known study, university students were asked to take notes during a lecture, either on a laptop or by hand. Those who used laptops wrote down more words, but they tended to copy what the lecturer said word for word. Those who wrote by hand had to be selective, and so they summarised the ideas in their own words. When they were tested afterwards, the students who had written by hand showed a better understanding of the ideas in the lecture. Lecturer: There's also research suggesting that young children who learn letters by writing them, rather than by typing them, are better at recognising those letters later. Some teachers also believe that children write longer and more imaginative stories when they use a pen rather than a keyboard, although this is harder to prove. And many of the people who take up calligraphy say that the main attraction is that it gives them a break from screens. Because it requires such careful concentration, it can be very relaxing, rather like meditation. Lecturer: Now let's go back in time and look at how people wrote in the past. The ancient Egyptians wrote on papyrus, a kind of paper made from a plant that grew along the River Nile. To write on it, they used pens made from reeds, which were cut at an angle and sometimes chewed at the end to make a kind of brush. Their ink was usually made from soot, mixed with water and a type of gum. Lecturer: In medieval Europe, the most common writing tool was the quill, a pen made from the feathers of large birds, especially geese. A good quill had to be cut very carefully with a small knife, and it needed to be sharpened again and again as the writer worked. That's where the word penknife comes from. Scribes in this period generally wrote on parchment, which was made from animal skin that had been cleaned, stretched and dried. It was very durable, but it was also very expensive, which is why writing was often very small, with no space wasted. Lecturer: The most widely used ink in Europe for over a thousand years was made from galls. These are small round growths that appear on oak trees when insects lay their eggs in them. When the galls were crushed and mixed with iron salts, they produced a dark ink that soaked into the page and lasted for centuries, although in some cases it has slowly eaten into the page. Lecturer: Of course, the invention of printing in the fifteenth century meant that books no longer had to be copied out by hand. But handwriting remained essential for letters, business and education for another five hundred years. Another interesting point is that, because people in so many different places were writing for so many different purposes, different regions developed their own scripts, with distinctive shapes of letters. This means that experts can often tell where and roughly when a manuscript was written simply by looking at the handwriting. We'll be looking at some examples of these scripts next week, and you'll have the chance to try some of them yourselves. Lecturer: So, before we move on, are there any questions so far? That is the end of Part 4. You now have one minute to check your answers to Part 4. That is the end of the listening test.
